A new proof of the theorems of Lin-Zaidenberg
and Abhyankar-Moh-SuzukiThanks: The author was supported by the Polish Ministry of Science and Higher Education, the Iuventus Plus grant, No. 0382/IP3/2013/72

Karol Palka Address: Karol Palka: Institute of Mathematics, Polish Academy of Sciences, ul. Śniadeckich 8, 00-656 Warsaw, Poland Email address: palka@impan.pl
Abstract.

Using the theory of minimal models of quasi-projective surfaces we give a new proof of the theorem of Lin-Zaidenberg which says that every topologically contractible algebraic curve in the complex affine plane has equation Xn=YmX^{n}=Y^{m} in some algebraic coordinates on the plane. This gives also a proof of the theorem of Abhyankar-Moh-Suzuki concerning embeddings of the complex line into the plane. Independently, we show how to deduce the latter theorem from basic properties of ℚ\mathbb{Q}-acyclic surfaces.

Key words and phrases: 
contractible curve, affine plane, Kodaira dimension, cusp
2000 Mathematics Subject Classification
Primary: 14H50; Secondary: 14R10

The following result is a homogeneous formulation of the theorems proved by Lin-Zaidenberg [ZL83] and Abhyankar-Moh [AM75] and Suzuki [Suz74]. Curves are assumed to be irreducible.

Theorem A.

If a complex algebraic curve in ℂ2\mathbb{C}^{2} is topologically contractible then in some algebraic coordinates {x,y}\{x,y\} on ℂ2\mathbb{C}^{2} its equation is xn=ymx^{n}=y^{m} for some coprime n>m>0n>m>0.

The part proved by Lin-Zaidenberg concerns singular curves (m≥2m\geq 2). The part proved by Abhyankar-Moh and Suzuki concerns smooth curves (m=1m=1) and is usually stated in the following form.

Theorem B.

If a complex algebraic curve in ℂ2\mathbb{C}^{2} is isomorphic to ℂ1\mathbb{C}^{1} then in some algebraic coordinates {x,y}\{x,y\} on ℂ2\mathbb{C}^{2} its equation is x=0x=0.

The Theorem B has now several published proofs using variety of methods, from algebraic to topological. The easiest we know is by Gurjar [Gur02]. As for the singular case of Theorem A, the original proof relies on Teichmüller theory. A topological proof based on properties of knots was given in [NR87, NR88]. Proofs of both theorems using algebraic geometry can be found in [GM96] and [Kor07]. The latter two use the tools of the theory of open algebraic surfaces including the logarithmic Bogomolov-Miyaoka-Yau inequality established for surfaces of log general type by Kobayashi [Kob90] and Kobayashi-Nakamura-Sakai [KNS89]. Our proof of Theorem A also uses the theory of minimal models for log surfaces. We believe it is quite short and geometric. Both theorems are deduced from the following result.

Theorem 1.

If A⊆ℂ2A\subseteq\mathbb{C}^{2} is a topologically contractible curve then there exists a minimal smooth completion (X,D)(X,D) of ℂ2∖A\mathbb{C}^{2}\setminus A, such that the proper transform of AA is a fiber of a ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1}-fibration of XX, whose restriction to ℂ2∖A\mathbb{C}^{2}\setminus A has irreducible fibers.

The basic new ingredient in the proof is to shift the focus from the surface ℂ2∖A\mathbb{C}^{2}\setminus A, where AA is the contractible curve, to the surface X=(ℂ2∖A)∪CX=(\mathbb{C}^{2}\setminus A)\cup C, where CC is (some naturally defined open subset of) the last (−1)(-1)-curve created by the minimal log resolution of the singularity at infinity (see section 1). While the boundary of XX is not any more connected, the important property is that in general the Euler characteristic of XX is negative. A similar idea was used in [PK13] and will be used in forthcoming papers (coauthored with M. Koras and P. Russell) finishing the classification of closed ℂ∗\mathbb{C}^{*}-embeddings into ℂ2\mathbb{C}^{2}. Another new ingredient is that we rely on a more general version of the log BMY inequality which works for surfaces of non-negative logarithmic Kodaira dimension. We tried to make the article self-contained. In section 3 we give an independent, direct proof of Theorem B using some basic properties of ℚ\mathbb{Q}-acyclic surfaces.

The author would like to thank Peter Russell and the referee for a careful reading of the preliminary version of the article.

1. Preliminaries and notation

We work in the category of complex algebraic varieties. The results of this section are well known, we give short proofs for completeness. Let D=∑i=1nDiD=\sum_{i=1}^{n}D_{i} be a reduced effective divisor on a smooth projective surface, which has smooth components DiD_{i} and only normal crossings (i.e. DD is an snc-divisor). The number of (irreducible) components of DD is denoted by #​D\#D. A component CC of DD is branching if it meets more then two components of D−CD-C. A (k)(k)-curve is a curve isomorphic to ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1} which has self-intersection kk. We say that DD is snc-minimal if after a contraction of any (−1)(-1)-curve contained in DD the image of DD is not an snc-divisor, or equivalently, if every (−1)(-1)-curve of DD is branching. We define the discriminant of DD by d⁡(D)=det(−[Di⋅Dj]i,j≤n)d(D)=\det(-[D_{i}\cdot D_{j}]_{i,j\leq n}). We put d⁡(0)=1d(0)=1.

A smooth pair (X¯,D)(\overline{X},D) consists of a smooth projective surface X¯\overline{X} and a reduced snc-divisor DD. If XX is a smooth quasi-projective surface then a smooth completion of XX is any smooth pair (X¯,D)(\overline{X},D) with a fixed identification X¯∖D≅X\overline{X}\setminus D\cong X. By ρ⁡(X¯)\rho(\overline{X}) we denote the Picard rank of X¯\overline{X}, which in case of rational surfaces is the same as dim⁡H2​(X¯,ℚ)\operatorname{dim}H_{2}(\overline{X},\mathbb{Q}). We check easily that the discriminant of DD and its total reduced transform under a blowing up are the same. Thus, for smooth completions of XX the discriminant d⁡(D)d(D) depends only on XX. In particular, if X=ℂ2X=\mathbb{C}^{2} then d⁡(D)=−1d(D)=-1. The following formula is a consequence of elementary properties of determinants.

Lemma 1.

Let T1T_{1} and T2T_{2} be reduced snc-divisors for which T1⋅T2=1T_{1}\cdot T_{2}=1 and let C1C_{1}, C2C_{2} be the unique components of T1T_{1} and T2T_{2} which meet. Then

(1.1) d⁡(T1+T2)=d⁡(T1)​d​(T2)−d⁡(T1−C1)​d​(T2−C2).d(T_{1}+T_{2})=d(T_{1})d(T_{2})-d(T_{1}-C_{1})d(T_{2}-C_{2}).

A ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1}- (a ℂ1\mathbb{C}^{1}-) fibration is a surjective morphism whose general fibers are isomorphic to ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1} (respectively to ℂ1\mathbb{C}^{1}). If (X¯,D)(\overline{X},D) is a smooth completion of XX and pp is some fixed ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1}-fibration of X¯\overline{X} we put ΣX=∑F⊄D(σ⁡(F)−1)\Sigma_{X}=\sum_{F\not\subset D}(\sigma(F)-1), where the sum is taken over all fibers of pp not contained in DD and σ⁡(F)\sigma(F) is the number of components of FF not contained in DD. Clearly, ΣX≥0\Sigma_{X}\geq 0 and the equality holds if and only if the restriction p|Xp_{|X} has irreducible fibers. Let ν\nu and hh be respectively the number of fibers contained in DD and the number of horizontal components of DD (i.e. these whose push-forward by pp does not vanish). The following lemma is due to Fujita [Fuj82, 4.16].

Lemma 2.

Let (X¯,D)(\overline{X},D) be a smooth completion of a smooth surface XX. With the above notation for every ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1}-fibration of X¯\overline{X} we have

(1.2) h+ν+ρ⁡(X¯)=ΣX+#​D+2.h+\nu+\rho(\overline{X})=\Sigma_{X}+\#D+2.
Proof.

Having a ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1}-fibration, X¯\overline{X} dominates some ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1}-bundle over a projective curve. The latter has ρ=2\rho=2, so we have ρ⁡(X¯)−2=∑F(#​F−1)=∑F#​F∩D+∑F(σ⁡(F)−1)=(#​D−h)+ΣX−ν.\rho(\overline{X})-2=\sum_{F}(\#F-1)=\sum_{F}\#F\cap D+\sum_{F}(\sigma(F)-1)=(\#D-h)+\Sigma_{X}-\nu. ∎

It is well known that every singular fiber of a ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1}-fibration of a smooth projective surface can be inductively reconstructed from a 00-curve by blowing up. In particular, we deduce by induction the following lemma.

Lemma 3.

Let FF be a reduction of a singular complete fiber of a ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1}-fibration of some smooth projective surface. Then FF is a rational snc-tree and its (−1)(-1)-curves are non-branching. Assume FF contains a unique (−1)(-1)-curve LFL_{F}. Then F−LFF-L_{F} has at most two connected components and if it has two then one of them is a chain of rational curves. Moreover, FF contains exactly two components of multiplicity 11, they are tips of FF and in case FF is not a chain they belong to the same connected component of F−LFF-L_{F}.

Note that sections meet only vertical components of multiplicity 11. We need a description of snc-minimal boundary divisors of ℂ2\mathbb{C}^{2}. We follow the proof by Daigle and Russell [Dai91, 5.12], [Rus02, §1] (which works for any surface completable by a chain). The lemma was originally proved by Ramanujam [Ram71] using only the fact that ℂ2\mathbb{C}^{2} is a smooth contractible surface which is simply connected at infinity.

Lemma 4.

If (X¯,D)(\overline{X},D) is a smooth snc-minimal completion of ℂ2\mathbb{C}^{2} then DD is a chain.

Proof.

First of all, consider a reduced divisor BB (on some smooth projective surface) which can be transformed into a 00-divisor by a sequence of blowups and blowdowns by taking reduced total transforms and push forwards. Assume also that D0D_{0} is either a zero divisor or a smooth curve not in BB, such that the transformation can be done modulo D0D_{0}, i.e. that under all steps of the process the proper transform of D0D_{0} is not contracted and stays smooth. We claim that BB contains a (−1)(-1)-curve in BB which is non-branching in D0+BD_{0}+B (in particular, D0+BD_{0}+B is not snc-minimal). To see this let B0B_{0} be the first component of BB which is contracted by the transformation, i.e. the transformation starts with a sequence of blowups and then it contracts the proper transform B0′B_{0}^{\prime} of B0B_{0}. If follows that B0′B_{0}^{\prime} is a (−1)(-1)-curve which is non-branching in the total reduced transform of D0+BD_{0}+B and hence that B0B_{0} is a curve with B02≥−1B_{0}^{2}\geq-1, non-branching in D0+BD_{0}+B. But the intersection matrix of BB, and hence of all its transforms, is negative definite, so B02=−1B_{0}^{2}=-1 and we are done.

Suppose DD has a branching component D0D_{0}. By the factorization theorem for birational morphisms between smooth projective surfaces we know that DD, being a boundary of ℂ2\mathbb{C}^{2}, can be transformed into a chain of rational curves. Therefore, there is a connected component BB of D−D0D-D_{0} which can be transformed to 00 modulo D0D_{0}. By the above argument there is a (−1)(-1)-curve B0B_{0} in BB which is non-branching in D0+BD_{0}+B. But then DD is not snc-minimal; a contradiction. ∎

The type of an ordered chain of rational curves T=T1+…+TkT=T_{1}+\ldots+T_{k} is the sequence [−T12,…,−Tk2][-T_{1}^{2},\ldots,-T_{k}^{2}]. We say that the chain is in a standard form if it is of type [0][0], [1][1] or [0,0,a1,…,ak−2][0,0,a_{1},\ldots,a_{k-2}] for some ai≥2a_{i}\geq 2. It is an elementary exercise to show that by blowing up and down on TT we can bring it into a standard form (the number of zeros is at most two by the Hodge index theorem). The formula 1.1 implies that if TT is a boundary of ℂ2\mathbb{C}^{2} in a standard form then it is of type [0,0][0,0].

An snc-divisor is of quotient type if it can be contracted algebraically to a quotient singularity, i.e. to a smooth or an isolated singular point which is locally analytically of type ℂ2/G\mathbb{C}^{2}/G, where GG is a finite subgroup of G​L​(2,ℂ)GL(2,\mathbb{C}). As a consequence, the intersection matrix of such a divisor is negative definite. Snc-minimal divisors of quotient type are well known, they are either negative definite chains of rational curves (corresponding to cyclic singularities ℂ2/ℤk\mathbb{C}^{2}/\mathbb{Z}_{k}) or special rational trees with unique branching components (forks). It is known that they do not contain (−1)(-1)-curves (see [Bri68]). For a general snc-divisor DD we denote the set of its connected components of quotient type by qt⁡(D)\operatorname{qt}(D).

Let (X¯,D)(\overline{X},D) be a smooth pair. For it we can run a minimal model program to obtain a birational morphism onto a log terminal surface (V,Δ)(V,\Delta) such that there is no curve LL on VV for which L2<0L^{2}<0 and L⋅(KV+Δ)<0L\cdot(K_{V}+\Delta)<0. The pair (V,Δ)(V,\Delta) is called a minimal model of (X¯,D)(\overline{X},D). If (X¯,D)(\overline{X},D) is snc-minimal (i.e. DD is an snc-minimal divisor) and the resulting morphism contracts only curves with supports in DD and its push-forwards then we say that (X¯,D)(\overline{X},D) is almost minimal (for another, more direct definition see [Miy01, §2.3.11]). Recall that a log resolution of a pair (V,Δ)(V,\Delta) with reduced Δ\Delta is a proper birational morphism from a smooth pair r:(X¯,D)→(V,Δ)r\colon(\overline{X},D)\to(V,\Delta) such that DD is the total reduced transform of Δ\Delta.

Let c⁡(D)c(D) denote the number of connected components of DD. The following proposition follows from [Fuj82, 6.20]. We denote the logarithmic Kodaira-Iitaka dimension by κ\kappa.

Proposition 5.

Let (X,D)(X,D) be a smooth snc-minimal pair which is not almost minimal. Then there exists a (−1)(-1)-curve ℓ\ell on XX which meets at most two connected components of DD, each at most once and transversally and for which κ⁡(X∖D)=κ⁡(X∖(D∪ℓ))\kappa(X\setminus D)=\kappa(X\setminus(D\cup\ell)). In particular, if p:(X,D)→(X′,D′)p\colon(X,D)\to(X^{\prime},D^{\prime}), with D′=p∗​DD^{\prime}=p_{*}D, is the contraction of ℓ\ell then

χ⁡(X′∖D′)+c⁡(D′)=χ⁡(X∖D)+c⁡(D)−1.\chi(X^{\prime}\setminus D^{\prime})+c(D^{\prime})=\chi(X\setminus D)+c(D)-1.

Note that (X′,D′)(X^{\prime},D^{\prime}) is a smooth pair and that if (X′,D′)(X^{\prime},D^{\prime}) is not snc-minimal then the sum χ⁡(X′∖D′)+c⁡(D′)\chi(X^{\prime}\setminus D^{\prime})+c(D^{\prime}) does not change when we snc-minimalize D′D^{\prime}.

2. Proof of Theorem 1

Assume that A⊆ℂ2A\subseteq\mathbb{C}^{2} is a topologically contractible curve. Let k≥0k\geq 0 be the number of singular points of AA. We write ℂ2\mathbb{C}^{2} as ℙ2∖L∞\mathbb{P}^{2}\setminus L_{\infty}, where L∞L_{\infty} is the line at infinity. Let A¯⊆ℙ2\bar{A}\subseteq\mathbb{P}^{2} be the closure AA and let

π:(X¯′,D′)→(ℙ2,L∞+A¯)\pi\colon(\overline{X}^{\prime},D^{\prime})\to(\mathbb{P}^{2},L_{\infty}+\bar{A})

be the minimal log resolution of singularities. We denote the proper transforms of A¯\bar{A} and L∞L_{\infty} on X¯′\overline{X}^{\prime} by EE and L∞′L_{\infty}^{\prime} respectively. Since the germ of A¯\bar{A} at infinity is analytically irreducible, the reduced total transform of L∞L_{\infty} contains a unique component C′C^{\prime} meeting EE. Moreover, their difference can be written as (π∗​L∞)r​e​d−C′=D1′+D2(\pi^{*}L_{\infty})_{red}-C^{\prime}=D_{1}^{\prime}+D_{2}, where D1′D_{1}^{\prime} and D2D_{2} are connected and D1′D_{1}^{\prime} contains L∞′L_{\infty}^{\prime}. We may, and shall, assume that A¯\bar{A} does not meet L∞L_{\infty} transversally, otherwise A¯\bar{A} is a line in which case the above theorems obviously hold. By the minimality of the resolution it follows that D2D_{2} is a rational chain with negative definite intersection matrix and with no (−1)(-1)-curves. In particular, d⁡(D2)≥2d(D_{2})\geq 2. Let UU be the reduced exceptional divisor over the singular points of AA. Put D3=E+UD_{3}=E+U. We have D′=D1′+C′+D2+D3D^{\prime}=D_{1}^{\prime}+C^{\prime}+D_{2}+D_{3}.

It may happen that L∞′L_{\infty}^{\prime} is a (−1)(-1)-curve (necessarily non-branching in D1′D_{1}^{\prime}). Moreover, its contraction may introduce new non-branching (−1)(-1)-curves in the boundary. Let

ψ:(X¯′,D′)→(X¯,D)\psi\colon(\overline{X}^{\prime},D^{\prime})\to(\overline{X},D)

be the composition of successive contractions of non-branching (−1)(-1)-curves contained in D1′D_{1}^{\prime} and its images. Put D1=ψ∗​D1D_{1}=\psi_{*}D_{1}, and C=ψ∗​C′C=\psi_{*}C^{\prime}. Since the curves contracted by ψ\psi are disjoint from D2+D3D_{2}+D_{3}, we denote D2D_{2}, EE, UU, D3D_{3} and their images on X¯\overline{X} by the same letters. We have D=D1+C+D2+D3D=D_{1}+C+D_{2}+D_{3}. Put

B=D1+D2+D3=D−C​ and ​X=X¯∖B.B=D_{1}+D_{2}+D_{3}=D-C\text{\ \ and\ \ }X=\overline{X}\setminus B.

Clearly, (X¯,D1+D2+D3)(\overline{X},D_{1}+D_{2}+D_{3}) is a smooth completion of XX and the DiD_{i}’s are the connected components of the boundary (it may happen that D1=0D_{1}=0). Also, X∖C=ℂ2∖AX\setminus C=\mathbb{C}^{2}\setminus A, with the smooth completion (X¯,D)(\overline{X},D). It follows that χ⁡(X)=χ⁡(ℂ2∖A)+χ⁡(C∖(D1∪D2∪E))=2−#​C∩(D1∪D2∪E)=−#​C∩D1.\chi(X)=\chi(\mathbb{C}^{2}\setminus A)+\chi(C\setminus(D_{1}\cup D_{2}\cup E))=2-\#C\cap(D_{1}\cup D_{2}\cup E)=-\#C\cap D_{1}. Thus, χ⁡(X)=−1\chi(X)=-1, unless D1=0D_{1}=0.

Because the log resolution π:(X¯′,D′)→(ℙ2,L∞+A¯)\pi\colon(\overline{X}^{\prime},D^{\prime})\to(\mathbb{P}^{2},L_{\infty}+\bar{A}) is minimal, each connected component of UU contains a unique component UiU_{i}, i=0,…,ki=0,\ldots,k, meeting EE. Moreover, each UiU_{i} is a (−1)(-1)-curve and Ui⋅E=1U_{i}\cdot E=1. The divisor BB is snc-minimal except the case when E2=−1E^{2}=-1 and UU has at most two connected components. Note however, that the minimality of the resolution implies that the only components of BB which meet EE are the (−1)(-1)-curves of UU. So, even if EE is a non-branching (−1)(-1)-curve in BB, its contraction does not introduce new non-branching (−1)(-1)-curves.

Proof of Theorem 1.
Claim 1.

If D1=0D_{1}=0 then Theorem 1 holds.

Proof.

We have C2≥(C′)2+1≥0C^{2}\geq(C^{\prime})^{2}+1\geq 0. Let DCD_{C} be the component of D2D_{2} meeting CC. Now (1.1) gives −C2​d​(D2)−d⁡(D2−DC)=−1-C^{2}d(D_{2})-d(D_{2}-D_{C})=-1, so C2​d​(D2)+d⁡(D2−DC)=1C^{2}d(D_{2})+d(D_{2}-D_{C})=1. Because d⁡(D2)≥2d(D_{2})\geq 2, we obtain C2=0C^{2}=0 and d⁡(D2−DC)=1d(D_{2}-D_{C})=1, hence D2D_{2} is irreducible. If we blow up once on E∩CE\cap C and contract the proper transform of CC the new boundary of XX has the same dual graph but the self-intersection of D2D_{2} increases. Repeating this elementary transformation we may assume D22=0D_{2}^{2}=0. Then the contraction of UU maps X¯\overline{X} to a smooth surface 𝔽\mathbb{F} with ρ=2\rho=2 and the linear system of (the proper transform of) D2D_{2} induces a projection p:𝔽→ℙ1p\colon\mathbb{F}\to\mathbb{P}^{1}. Moreover, (the proper transform of) EE is disjoint from D2D_{2}, so it is a 00-curve. Then U=0U=0 and Theorem 1 holds. ∎

Thus from now on we assume D1≠0D_{1}\neq 0 (and D2≠0D_{2}\neq 0).

Claim 2.

There is no curve ℓ⊈D1+D2+U\ell\not\subseteq D_{1}+D_{2}+U for which the intersection matrix of ℓ+D1+D2+U\ell+D_{1}+D_{2}+U is negative definite.

Proof.

We have #⁡(ℓ+D1+D2+U)=#​D−1=ρ⁡(X¯)\#(\ell+D_{1}+D_{2}+U)=\#D-1=\rho(\overline{X}), so the claim follows from the Hodge index theorem. ∎

Claim 3.

If D1D_{1} is not negative definite then it is not a chain and CC is a (−1)(-1)-curve.

Proof.

Suppose D1D_{1} is a chain. We change it into a standard form D~1\tilde{D}_{1}, so that the zero-curve is a tip of DD. Denote the proper transform of CC by C~\tilde{C}. If D~1\tilde{D}_{1} is irreducible then it is a 00-curve, so by (1.1) −1=d⁡(D~1+C~+D2)=−d⁡(D2)≤−2-1=d(\tilde{D}_{1}+\tilde{C}+D_{2})=-d(D_{2})\leq-2, which is impossible. Thus D~1\tilde{D}_{1} is not irreducible. Then E+C~+D2E+\tilde{C}+D_{2} is vertical for the ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1}-fibration induced by the 00-tip, so either C~\tilde{C} is a branching component of a fiber or it meets two components of a fiber and the section contained in D~1\tilde{D}_{1}. By Lemma 3 C~\tilde{C} cannot be a (−1)(-1)-curve, hence (C~)2≤−2(\tilde{C})^{2}\leq-2. Then D~1+C~+D2\tilde{D}_{1}+\tilde{C}+D_{2} is a boundary of ℂ2\mathbb{C}^{2} in a standard form, so it is of type [0,0][0,0]. But then D2=0D_{2}=0; a contradiction. Thus D1D_{1} is not a chain. By Lemma 4 D1+C+D2D_{1}+C+D_{2} is not snc-minimal, so C2=−1C^{2}=-1. ∎

Claim 4.

D3D_{3} is not a (−1)(-1)-curve.

Proof.

Suppose D3D_{3} is a (−1)(-1)-curve. Then U=0U=0 and D3=ED_{3}=E. Taking ℓ=E\ell=E in Claim 2 we see that D1D_{1} is not negative definite. By Claim 3 D1D_{1} is not a chain and CC is a (−1)(-1)-curve. Consider the ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1}-fibration given by the linear system of E+CE+C. We have h=2h=2, so ΣX=ν\Sigma_{X}=\nu. The divisor BB contains no fibers. Indeed, otherwise DD would contain more than one fiber (E+CE+C is one of them), hence DD would contain a loop, which is false. We obtain ΣX=ν=0\Sigma_{X}=\nu=0. Let FF be a singular fiber and LFL_{F} its unique component not contained in BB. The two sections contained in BB belong to different connected components of BB, so the two components of FF of multiplicity one meeting them belong to different connected components of F−LFF-L_{F}. By Lemma 3 it follows that FF is a chain and meets the sections in tips. Since the vertical part of D2D_{2} is connected, there is at most one singular fiber other than E+CE+C. It follows that D1D_{1} is a chain; a contradiction. ∎

Claim 5.

If U≠0U\neq 0 then D3D_{3} is not contained in a divisor of quotient type.

Proof.

Suppose QQ is a divisor of quotient type containing D3D_{3}. The (−1)(-1)-curve U1U_{1} is branching in D3D_{3}, hence in QQ. Because the self-intersection of U1U_{1} is (−1)(-1), the snc-minimalization of QQ does not touch U1U_{1}, hence leads to an snc-minimal divisor of quotient type which contains a branching (−1)(-1)-curve. But there are no such divisors. A contradiction. ∎

We now analyze the creation of the almost minimal model of (X¯,B)(\overline{X},B). Let ϵ\epsilon be the contraction of EE in case it is a non-branching (−1)(-1)-curve, otherwise put ϵ=idX¯\epsilon=\operatorname{id}_{\overline{X}}. Let

(X¯,B)→ϵ(X¯0,B0)→p1(X¯1,B1)→p2…→pn(X¯n,Bn)(\overline{X},B)\xrightarrow{\epsilon}(\overline{X}_{0},B_{0})\xrightarrow{p_{1}}(\overline{X}_{1},B_{1})\xrightarrow{p_{2}}\ldots\xrightarrow{p_{n}}(\overline{X}_{n},B_{n})

be a sequence of birational morphism leading to the almost minimal model (X¯n,Bn)(\overline{X}_{n},B_{n}) of (X¯,B)(\overline{X},B) grouped so that pi+1p_{i+1} is a composition of a contraction of some (−1)(-1)-curve ℓi⊈Bi\ell_{i}\not\subseteq B_{i} witnessing the non-almost minimalisty of (X¯i,Bi)(\overline{X}_{i},B_{i}) followed by the snc-minimalization of the image of BiB_{i}. Put p=pn∘…∘p1∘εp=p_{n}\circ\ldots\circ p_{1}\circ\varepsilon and Xi=X¯i∖BiX_{i}=\overline{X}_{i}\setminus B_{i}. We denote ℓi\ell_{i}’s and their proper transforms on X¯\overline{X} by the same letters.

Claim 6.

χ⁡(X)=χ⁡(X0)\chi(X)=\chi(X_{0}) and χ⁡(Xi)≥χ⁡(Xi+1)\chi(X_{i})\geq\chi(X_{i+1}).

Proof.

Claim 8.

3. Another proof of the Abhyankar-Moh-Suzuki theorem

We now give another, independent of section 2, proof of Theorem B. We need the following lemma. In case of contractible surfaces it was obtained by similar methods by Gurjar and Miyanishi [GM98].

Lemma 6.

[Pal13, 3.1(vii)] Let X→X′X\to X^{\prime} be a log resolution of a rational ℚ\mathbb{Q}-acyclic normal surface, let E^\widehat{E} be the reduced exceptional divisor and (X¯,D)(\overline{X},D) a smooth completion of XX. If E^+D\widehat{E}+D is a sum of rational trees then

|d⁡(D)|=d⁡(E^)⋅|H1​(X′,ℤ)|2.|d(D)|=d(\widehat{E})\cdot|H_{1}(X^{\prime},\mathbb{Z})|^{2}.
Proof.

Let MDM_{D} and MM be the boundaries of closures of tubular neighborhoods of DD and E^\widehat{E}. We may assume that MDM_{D} and MM are disjoint oriented 3-manifolds. Since E^\widehat{E} is a sum of rational trees, H1​(E^,ℚ)=0H_{1}(\widehat{E},\mathbb{Q})=0. By the ℚ\mathbb{Q}-acyclicity of X′X^{\prime} the components of D+E^D+\widehat{E} freely generate H2​(X¯,ℚ)H_{2}(\overline{X},\mathbb{Q}), so d⁡(D+E^)≠0d(D+\widehat{E})\neq 0. By [Mum61] H1​(MD,ℤ)H_{1}(M_{D},\mathbb{Z}) and H1​(M,ℤ)H_{1}(M,\mathbb{Z}) are finite groups of orders respectively |d⁡(D)||d(D)| and d⁡(E^)d(\widehat{E}). By the Poincare duality H2​(MD,ℤ)H_{2}(M_{D},\mathbb{Z}) and H2​(M,ℤ)H_{2}(M,\mathbb{Z}) are trivial. Let K=X¯∖(T​u​b​(D)∪T​u​b​(E^))K=\overline{X}\setminus(Tub(D)\cup Tub(\widehat{E})). By the Lefschetz duality Hi​(K,MD)≅H4−i​(K,M)=H4−i​(X′,Sing⁡X′),H_{i}(K,M_{D})\cong H^{4-i}(K,M)=H^{4-i}(X^{\prime},\operatorname{Sing}\ X^{\prime}), which for i>1i>1 implies that Hi​(K,MD)≅H4−i​(X′)≅H3−i​(X′)H_{i}(K,M_{D})\cong H^{4-i}(X^{\prime})\cong H_{3-i}(X^{\prime}) by the universal coefficient formula. Thus the reduced homology exact sequence of the pair (K,MD)(K,M_{D}) with ℤ\mathbb{Z}-coefficients gives:

0→H2​(K)→H1​(X′)→H1​(MD)→H1​(K)→H2​(X′)→0.0\xrightarrow{\ \ }H_{2}(K)\xrightarrow{\ \ }H_{1}(X^{\prime})\xrightarrow{\ \ }H_{1}(M_{D})\xrightarrow{\ \ }H_{1}(K)\xrightarrow{\ \ }H_{2}(X^{\prime})\xrightarrow{\ \ }0.

On the other hand, since Hi​(K,M)≅Hi​(X′,Sing⁡X′)H_{i}(K,M)\cong H_{i}(X^{\prime},\operatorname{Sing}\ X^{\prime}) and H1​(X′,Sing⁡X′)=H1​(X′)⊕H~0​(Sing⁡X′)H_{1}(X^{\prime},\operatorname{Sing}\ X^{\prime})=H_{1}(X^{\prime})\oplus\widetilde{H}_{0}(\operatorname{Sing}X^{\prime}), the reduced homology exact sequence of the pair (K,M)(K,M) gives:

0→H2​(K)→H2​(X′)→H1​(M)→H1​(K)→H1​(X′)→0.0\xrightarrow{\ \ }H_{2}(K)\xrightarrow{\ \ }H_{2}(X^{\prime})\xrightarrow{\ \ }H_{1}(M)\xrightarrow{\ \ }H_{1}(K)\xrightarrow{\ \ }H_{1}(X^{\prime})\xrightarrow{\ \ }0.

From the two exact sequences we obtain |H2​(K)|⋅|d⁡(D)|⋅|H2​(X′)|=|H1​(X′)|⋅|H1​(K)||H_{2}(K)|\cdot|d(D)|\cdot|H_{2}(X^{\prime})|=|H_{1}(X^{\prime})|\cdot|H_{1}(K)| and |H2​(K)|⋅d⁡(E^)⋅|H1​(X′)|=|H2​(X′)|⋅|H1​(K)||H_{2}(K)|\cdot d(\widehat{E})\cdot|H_{1}(X^{\prime})|=|H_{2}(X^{\prime})|\cdot|H_{1}(K)|, hence

|d⁡(D)|⋅|H2​(X′,ℤ)|2=d⁡(E^)⋅|H1​(X′,ℤ)|2.|d(D)|\cdot|H_{2}(X^{\prime},\mathbb{Z})|^{2}=d(\widehat{E})\cdot|H_{1}(X^{\prime},\mathbb{Z})|^{2}.

Because a rational ℚ\mathbb{Q}-acyclic surface is necessarily affine by an argument of Fujita ([Fuj82, 2.4]), XX is an affine variety, and hence has a structure of a CW-complex of real dimension 22. It follows that H2​(X′,ℤ)H_{2}(X^{\prime},\mathbb{Z}) is torsionless, hence H2​(X′,ℤ)=0H_{2}(X^{\prime},\mathbb{Z})=0.

Assume A⊆ℂ2A\subseteq\mathbb{C}^{2} is a smooth contractible planar curve. Let (X¯,D)(\overline{X},D) be a completion of ℂ2∖A\mathbb{C}^{2}\setminus A defined in section 2.
